Florida's first recorded attempt to assess real estate at its full value, coupled with the announcement of City Tax Assessor Sam Pinder that he would follow suit, has given the Monroe county Key West taxpayer the simplest basis for comparison ever granted him.


Because the per cent of valuation has not always been made known in the past, it has been difficult for the taxpayer to know exactly what comparison to make between the figures of the city and county departments.


Now, however, with both departments assessing the property at its 100 per cent valuation, it would seem that the two sets of books would vary only in so much as the natural difference of opinion between the two officers.


But that doesn't seem to be the case.


Tax Assessor Gandolfo, County, has assessed the entire real estate valuation of Key West, excluding all property outside the city limits, at $8,726,060.


Tax Assessor Pinder (city) figured the same property on the same basis at $7,198,470.


That is a difference of opinion amounting to close to 15 per cent, which, in turn, means that when Gandolfo marks down a house at $10,000 Pinder has it down for $8,500; when Gandolfo has one down for $125,900, Pinder, if he listed that one, would have it down for $102,500, or $23,400 less.


Since almost all of the Monroe county taxpayers also pay taxes to Key West, that great difference between the two books provides reasonable subject for speculation.


Some of the taxpayers have speculated, for instance, that pieces of Key West property listed by the county are not on the city books.


A joint committee of the council and commission probably could determine why there is so much difference in procedure which could eliminate speculation as well as avoiding inevitable resentment.
